claims.text: Rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys can exhibit a magnetocaloric response near a magnetic transition temperature.
Standard slow cooling produces a relatively homogeneous microstructure in the target alloy.
Accelerated cooling during solidification induces microstructural heterogeneity.
Accelerated cooling refines the alloy's grain size.
Accelerated cooling creates controlled nanoscale defect structures.
Refined grains, twin boundaries, and nanoscale defects act as efficient nucleation sites for magnetic-domain reorientation near the Curie point.
Processing-induced heterogeneity reduces local energy barriers for magnetic-domain reorientation.
Processing-induced heterogeneity modifies exchange interactions in a way that facilitates the magnetocaloric effect.
Rapidly solidified samples will have a higher magnetic entropy change than slow-cooled samples under fields below 1 T near the Curie temperature.
Rapidly solidified samples will have lower magnetic hysteresis losses than slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly solidified samples will maintain or improve heat-exchange efficiency relative to slow-cooled samples.
Rapidly solidified samples will maintain or improve mechanical stability relative to slow-cooled samples.
There is a cooling-rate window that produces microstructural refinement without amorphization or excessive residual stress.
Cooling rates above a threshold can produce deleterious microstructural instabilities.
The optimal balance between induced heterogeneity and mechanical stability depends on alloy composition and processing conditions.
Identically composed rapid-solidification and slow-cooling sample sets provide the controlled comparison needed to test the hypothesis.
